entries.0da9ae972618733c266d091956c0f02c8964867e: <div sID="gen9911" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="28" osisID="Job.28" sID="Job.28"/> <div eID="gen9911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9912" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9913" type="x-p"/> The strain of this chapter is very unlike the rest of this book. Job forgets his sores, and all his sorrows, and talks like a philosopher or a virtuoso. Here is a great deal both of natural and moral philosophy in this discourse; but the question is, How does it come in here? Doubtless it was not merely for an amusement, or diversion from the controversy; though, if it had been only so, perhaps it would not have been much amiss. When disputes grow hot, better lose the question than lose our temper. But this is pertinent and to the business in hand. Job and his friends had been discoursing about the dispensations of Providence towards the wicked and the righteous. Job had shown that some wicked men live and die in prosperity, while others are presently and openly arrested by the judgments of God. But, if any ask the reason why some are punished in this world and not others, they must be told it is a question that cannot be answered. The knowledge of the reasons of state in God's government of the world is kept from us, and we must neither pretend to it nor reach after it. Zophar had wished that God would show Job the "secrets of wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Job.11.6">ch. xi. 6</reference>). No, says Job, "secret things belong not to us, but things revealed," <reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">Deut. xxix. 29</reference>. And here he shows, I. Concerning worldly wealth, how industriously that is sought for and pursued by the children of men, what pains they take, what contrivances they have, and what hazards they run to get it, <reference osisRef="Job.28.1-Job.28.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. Concerning wisdom, <reference osisRef="Job.28.12">ver. 12</reference>. In general, the price of it is very great; it is of inestimable value, <reference osisRef="Job.28.15-Job.28.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. The place of it is very secret, <reference osisRef="Job.28.14">ver. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.20">20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.22">22</reference>. In particular, there is a wisdom which is hidden in God (<reference osisRef="Job.28.23-Job.28.27">ver. 23-27</reference>) and there is a wisdom which is revealed to the children of men, <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">ver. 28</reference>. Our enquiries into the former must be checked, into the latter quickened, for that is it which is our concern.
entries.4dca744a6e831124ad65f44c43513e96dbc09835: <div eID="gen9913" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9912" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Extent of Human Discoveries. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9914" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold <hi type="italic">where</hi> they fine <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> Iron is taken out of the earth, and brass <hi type="italic">is</hi> molten <hi type="italic">out of</hi> the stone. <hi type="super">3</hi> He setteth an end to darkness, and searcheth out all perfection: the stones of darkness, and the shadow of death. <hi type="super">4</hi> The flood breaketh out from the inhabitant; <hi type="italic">even the waters</hi> forgotten of the foot: they are dried up, they are gone away from men. <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> the earth, out of it cometh bread: and under it is turned up as it were fire. <hi type="super">6</hi> The stones of it <hi type="italic">are</hi> the place of sapphires: and it hath dust of gold. <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen: <hi type="super">8</hi> The lion's whelps have not trodden it, nor the fierce lion passed by it. <hi type="super">9</hi> He putteth forth his hand upon the rock; he overturneth the mountains by the roots. <hi type="super">10</hi> He cutteth out rivers among the rocks; and his eye seeth every precious thing. 11 He bindeth the floods from overflowing; and <hi type="italic">the thing that is</hi> hid bringeth he forth to light. <hi type="super">12</hi> But where shall wisdom be found? and where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the place of understanding? <hi type="super">13</hi> Man knoweth not the price thereof; neither is it found in the land of the living. <div eID="gen9914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9915" type="x-p"/> Here Job shows, 1. What a great way the wit of man may go in diving into the depths of nature and seizing the riches of it, what a great deal of knowledge and wealth men may, by their ingenious and industrious searches, make themselves masters of. But does it therefore follow that men may, by their wit, comprehend the reasons why some wicked people prosper and others are punished, why some good people prosper and others are afflicted? No, by no means. The caverns of the earth may be discovered, but not the counsels of heaven. 2. What a great deal of care and pains worldly men take to get riches. He had observed concerning the wicked man (<reference osisRef="Job.27.16">ch. xxvii. 16</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">heaped up silver as the dust;</hi> now here he shows whence that silver came which he was so fond of and how it was obtained, to show what little reason wicked rich men have to be proud of their wealth and pomp. Observe here, <div eID="gen9915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9916" type="x-p"/> I. The wealth of this world is hidden in the earth. Thence the silver and the gold, which afterwards they refine, are fetched, <reference osisRef="Job.28.1">v. 1</reference>. There they lay mixed with a great deal of dirt and dross, like a worthless thing, of no more account than common earth; and abundance of them will so lie neglected, till the earth and all the works therein shall be burnt up. Holy Mr. Herbert, in his poem called <hi type="italic">Avarice,</hi> takes notice of this, to shame men out of the love of money:— <div eID="gen9916" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9917"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9918"/>Money, thou bane of bliss, thou source of woe,<l eID="gen9918" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9919"/>Whence com'st thou, that thou art so fresh and fine?<l eID="gen9919" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9920"/>I know thy parentage is base and low;<l eID="gen9920" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9921"/>Man found thee poor and dirty in a mine.<l eID="gen9921" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9922"/>Surely thou didst so little contribute<l eID="gen9922" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9923"/>To this great kingdom which thou now hast got<l eID="gen9923" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9924"/>That he was fain, when thou wast destitute,<l eID="gen9924" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9925"/>To dig thee out of thy dark cave and grot.<l eID="gen9925" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9926"/>Man calleth thee his wealth, who made thee rich,<l eID="gen9926" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9927"/>And while he digs out thee falls in the ditch.<l eID="gen9927" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9917"/> <div sID="gen9928" type="x-p"/> Iron and brass, less costly but more serviceable metals, are <hi type="italic">taken out of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.2">v. 2</reference>), and are there found in great abundance, which abates their price indeed, but is a great kindness to man, who could much better be without gold than without iron. Nay, <hi type="italic">out of the earth comes bread,</hi> that is, bread-corn, the necessary support of life, <reference osisRef="Job.28.5">v. 5</reference>. Thence man's maintenance is fetched, to remind him of his own original; he is of the earth, and is hastening to the earth. <hi type="italic">Under it is turned up as it were fire,</hi> precious stones, that sparkle as fire—brimstone, that is apt to take fire—coal, that is proper to feed fire. As we have our food, so we have our fuel, out of the earth. There the sapphires and other gems are, and thence gold-dust is digged up;, <reference osisRef="Job.28.6">v. 6</reference>. The wisdom of the Creator has placed these things, 1. Out of our sight, to teach us not to set our eyes upon them, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>. 2. Under our feet, to teach us not to lay them in our bosoms, nor to set our hearts upon them, but to trample upon them with a holy contempt. See how full the <hi type="italic">earth is of God's riches</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.24">Ps. civ. 24</reference>) and infer thence, not only how great a God he is <hi type="italic">whose the earth is</hi> and <hi type="italic">the fulness thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Ps. xxiv. 1</reference>), but how full heaven must needs be of God's riches, which is the city of the great King, in comparison with which this earth is a poor country. <div eID="gen9928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9929" type="x-p"/> II. The wealth that is hidden in the earth cannot be obtained but with a great deal of difficulty. 1. It is hard to be found out: there is but here and there <hi type="italic">a vein for the silver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.1">v. 1</reference>. The precious stones, though bright themselves, yet, because buried in obscurity and out of sight, are called <hi type="italic">stones of darkness and the shadow of death.</hi> Men may search long before they light on them. 2. When found out it is hard to be fetched out. Men's wits must be set on work to contrive ways and means to get this hidden treasure into their hands. They must with their lamps <hi type="italic">set an end to darkness;</hi> and if one expedient miscarry, one method fail, they must try another, till they have <hi type="italic">searched out all perfection,</hi> and turned every stone to effect it, <reference osisRef="Job.28.3">v. 3</reference>. They must grapple with subterraneous waters (<reference osisRef="Job.28.4">v. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.10">10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.11">11</reference>), and force their way through rocks which are, as it were, the roots of the mountains, <reference osisRef="Job.28.9">v. 9</reference>. Now God has made the getting of gold, and silver, and precious stones, so difficult, (1.) For the exciting and engaging of industry. <hi type="italic">Dii laboribus omnia vendunt—Labour is the price which the gods affix to all things.</hi> If valuable things were too easily obtained men would never learn to take pains. But the difficulty of gaining the riches of this earth may suggest to us what violence the kingdom of heaven suffers. (2.) For the checking and restraining of pomp and luxury. What is for necessity is had with a little labour from the surface of the earth; but what is for ornament must be dug with a great deal of pains out of the bowels of it. To be fed is cheap, but to be fine is chargeable. <div eID="gen9929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> III. Though the subterraneous wealth is thus hard to obtain, yet men will have it. He that loves silver is not satisfied with silver, and yet is not satisfied without it; but those that have much must needs have more. See here, 1. What inventions men have to get this wealth. They <hi type="italic">search out all perfection,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.3">v. 3</reference>. They have arts and engines to dry up the waters, and carry them off, when they break in upon them in their mines and threaten to drown the work, <reference osisRef="Job.28.4">v. 4</reference>. They have pumps, and pipes, and canals, to clear their way, and, obstacles being removed, they tread <hi type="italic">the path which no fowl knoweth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.7-Job.28.8">v. 7, 8</reference>), unseen by the vulture's eye, which is piercing and quick-sighted, and untrodden by the lion's whelps, which traverse all the paths of the wilderness. 2. What pains men take, and what vast charge they are at, to get this wealth. They work their way through the rocks and undermine the mountains, <reference osisRef="Job.28.10">v. 10</reference>. 3. What hazards they run. Those that dig in the mines have their lives in their hands; for they are obliged to <hi type="italic">bind the floods from overflowing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.11">v. 11</reference>), and are continually in danger of being suffocated by damps or crushed or buried alive by the fall of the earth upon them. See how foolish man adds to his own burden. He is sentenced to eat bread in the sweat of his face; but, as if that were not enough, he will get gold and silver at the peril of his life, though the more is gotten the less valuable it is. In Solomon's time silver was as stones. But, 4. Observe what it is that carries men through all this toil and peril: <hi type="italic">Their eye sees every precious thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.10">v. 10</reference>. Silver and gold are precious things with them, and they have them in their eye in all these pursuits. They fancy they see them glittering before their faces, and, in the prospect of laying hold of them, they make nothing of all these difficulties; for they make something of their toil at last: <hi type="italic">That which is hidden bringeth he forth to light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.11">v. 11</reference>. What was hidden under ground is laid upon the bank; the metal that was hidden in the ore is refined from its dross and brought forth pure out of the furnace; and then he thinks his pains well bestowed. Go to the miners then, thou sluggard in religion; consider their ways, and be wise. Let their courage, diligence, and constancy in seeking the wealth that perisheth shame us out of slothfulness and faint-heartedness in labouring for the true riches. <hi type="italic">How much better is it to get wisdom than gold!</hi> How much easier and safer! Yet gold is sought for, but grace neglected. Will the hopes of <hi type="italic">precious things</hi> out of the earth (so they call them, though really they are paltry and perishing) be such a spur to industry, and shall not the certain prospect of truly precious things in heaven be much more so?
entries.852ef30b5a5fcfec787a03d91302388d5b455f15: <div eID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Excellency of Wisdom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The depth saith, It <hi type="italic">is</hi> not in me: and the sea saith, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> not with me. <hi type="super">15</hi> It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed <hi type="italic">for</hi> the price thereof. <hi type="super">16</hi> It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire. <hi type="super">17</hi> The gold and the crystal cannot equal it: and the exchange of it <hi type="italic">shall not be for</hi> jewels of fine gold. <hi type="super">18</hi> No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> above rubies. <hi type="super">19</hi> The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it, neither shall it be valued with pure gold. <div eID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> Job, having spoken of the wealth of the world, which men put such a value upon and take so much pains for, here comes to speak of another more valuable jewel, and that is, <hi type="italic">wisdom and understanding,</hi> the knowing and enjoying of God and ourselves. Those that found out all those ways and means to enrich themselves thought themselves very wise; but Job will not own theirs to be wisdom. He supposes them to gain their point, and to bring to light what they sought for (<reference osisRef="Job.28.11">v. 11</reference>), and yet asks, "<hi type="italic">Where is wisdom?</hi> for it is not here." This their way is their folly. We must therefore seek it somewhere else, and it will be found nowhere but in the principles and practices of religion. There is more true knowledge, satisfaction, and happiness, in sound divinity, which shows us the way to the joys of heaven, than in natural philosophy or mathematics, which help us to find a way into the bowels of the earth. Two things cannot be found out concerning this wisdom:— <div eID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9933" type="x-p"/> I. The price of it, for that is inestimable; its worth is infinitely more than all the riches in this world: <hi type="italic">Man knows not the price thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.13">v. 13</reference>), that is, 1. Few put a due value upon it. Men know not the worth of it, its innate excellency, their need of it, and of what unspeakable advantage it will be to them; and therefore, though they have many a price in their hand to get this wisdom, yet they <hi type="italic">have no heart to it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.16">Prov. xvii. 16</reference>. The cock in the fable knew not the value of the precious stone he found in the dunghill, and therefore would rather have lighted on a barley-corn. Men know not the worth of grace, and therefore will take no pains to get it. 2. None can possibly give a valuable consideration for it, with all the wealth this world can furnish them with. This Job enlarges upon <reference osisRef="Job.28.15-Job.28.19">v. 15</reference>, &c., where he makes an inventory of the <hi type="italic">bona notabilia—the most valuable treasures</hi> of this world. Gold is five times mentioned; silver comes in also; and then several precious stones, the onyx and sapphire, pearls and rubies, and the topaz of Ethiopia. These are the things that are highest prized in the world's markets: but if a man would give, not only these, heaps of these, but all the substance of his house, all he is worth in the world, for wisdom, it would utterly be contemned. These may give a man some advantage in seeking wisdom, as they did to Solomon, but there is no purchasing wisdom with these. It is a gift of <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost,</hi> which <hi type="italic">cannot be bought with money,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.8.20">Acts viii. 20</reference>. As it does not run in the blood, and so come to us by descent, so it cannot be got for money, nor does it come to us by purchase. Spiritual gifts are conferred without money and without price, because no money can be a price for them. Wisdom is likewise a more valuable gift to him that has it, makes him richer and happier, than gold or precious stones. It is <hi type="italic">better to get wisdom than gold.</hi> Gold is another's, wisdom our own; gold is for the body and time, wisdom for the soul and eternity. Let that which is most precious in God's account be so in ours. See <reference osisRef="Prov.3.14-Prov.3.20">Prov. iii. 14</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen9933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9934" type="x-p"/> II. The place of it, for that is undiscoverable. <hi type="italic">Where shall wisdom be found?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.12">v. 12</reference>. He asks this, 1. As one that truly desired to find it. This is a question we should all put. While the most of men are asking, "Where shall money be found?" we should ask, <hi type="italic">Where may wisdom be found?</hi> that we may seek it and find it, not vain philosophy, or carnal policy, but true religion; for that is the only true wisdom, that is it which best improves our faculties and best secures our spiritual and eternal welfare. This is that which we should cry after and dig for, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.3-Prov.2.4">Prov. ii. 3, 4</reference>. 2. As one that utterly despaired of finding it any where but in God, and any way but by divine revelation: <hi type="italic">It is not found in</hi> this <hi type="italic">land of the living,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.13">v. 13</reference>. We cannot attain to a right understanding of God and his will, of ourselves and our duty and interest, by reading any books or men, but by reading God's book and the men of God. Such is the degeneracy of human nature that there is no true wisdom to be found with any but those who are born again, and who, through grace, partake of the divine nature. As for others, even the most ingenious and industrious, they can tell us no tidings of this lost wisdom. (1.) Ask the miners, and by them <hi type="italic">the depth will say, It is not in me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.14">v. 14</reference>. Those who dig into the bowels of the earth, to rifle the treasures there, cannot in these dark recesses find this rare jewel, nor with all their art make themselves masters of it. (2.) Ask the mariners, and by them <hi type="italic">the sea will say, It is not in me.</hi> It can never be got either by trading on the waters or diving into them, can never be <hi type="italic">sucked from the abundance of the seas or the treasures hidden in the sand.</hi> Where there is a vein for the silver there is no vein for wisdom, none for grace. Men can more easily break through the difficulties they meet with in getting worldly wealth than through those they meet with in getting heavenly wisdom, and they will take more pains to learn how to live in this world than how to live for ever in a better world. So blind and foolish has man become that it is in vain to ask him, <hi type="italic">Where is the place of wisdom,</hi> and which is the road that leads to it?
entries.07ee9fe866ab4df78148ff017ff064c3b1696d22: <div eID="gen9934" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Wisdom Hidden from Man; The Wisdom Revealed to Man. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9935" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Whence then cometh wisdom? and where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the place of understanding? <hi type="super">21</hi> Seeing it is hid from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the fowls of the air. <hi type="super">22</hi> Destruction and death say, We have heard the fame thereof with our ears. <hi type="super">23</hi> God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof. <hi type="super">24</hi> For he looketh to the ends of the earth, <hi type="italic">and</hi> seeth under the whole heaven; <hi type="super">25</hi> To make the weight for the winds; and he weigheth the waters by measure. <hi type="super">26</hi> When he made a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunder: <hi type="super">27</hi> Then did he see it, and declare it; he prepared it, yea, and searched it out. <hi type="super">28</hi> And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> wisdom; and to depart from evil <hi type="italic">is</hi> understanding. <div eID="gen9935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9936" type="x-p"/> The question which Job had asked (<reference osisRef="Job.28.12">v. 12</reference>) he asks again here; for it is too worthy, too weighty, to be let fall, until we speed in the enquiry. Concerning this we must seek till we find, till we get some satisfactory account of it. By a diligent prosecution of this enquiry he brings it, at length, to this issue, that there is a twofold wisdom, one <hi type="italic">hidden in God,</hi> which is secret and <hi type="italic">belongs not to us,</hi> the other made known by him and revealed to man, which <hi type="italic">belongs to us and to our children.</hi> <div eID="gen9936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9937" type="x-p"/> I. The knowledge of God's secret will, the will of his providence, is out of our reach, and what God has reserved to himself. It <hi type="italic">belongs to the Lord our God.</hi> To know the particulars of what God will do hereafter, and the reasons of what he is doing now, is the knowledge Job first speaks of. <div eID="gen9937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9938" type="x-p"/> 1. This knowledge is hidden from us. It is high, we cannot attain unto it (<reference osisRef="Job.28.21-Job.28.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is hid from the eyes of all living,</hi> even of philosophers, politicians, and saints; it is <hi type="italic">kept close from the fowls of the air;</hi> though they fly high and in the open firmament of heaven, though they seem somewhat nearer that upper world where the source of this wisdom is, though their eyes behold afar off (<reference osisRef="Job.39.29">ch. xxxix. 29</reference>), yet they cannot penetrate into the counsels of God. No, man is <hi type="italic">wiser than the fowls of heaven,</hi> and yet comes short of this wisdom. Even those who, in their speculations, soar highest, and think themselves, like the fowls of the air, above the heads of other people, yet cannot pretend to this knowledge. Job and his friends had been arguing about the methods and reasons of the dispensations of Providence in the government of the world. "What fools are we" (says Job) "to fight in the dark thus, to dispute about that which we do not understand!" The line and plummet of human reason can never fathom the abyss of the divine counsels. Who can undertake to give the rationale of Providence, or account for the maxims, measure, and methods of God's government, those <hi type="italic">arcana imperii—cabinet counsels</hi> of divine wisdom? Let us then be content not to know the future events of the Providence until time discover them (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Acts i. 7</reference>) and not to know the secret reasons of Providence until eternity discover them. God is now a God that hideth himself (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa. xlv. 15</reference>); <hi type="italic">clouds and darkness are round about him.</hi> Though this wisdom be hidden from all living, yet <hi type="italic">destruction and death say, We have heard the fame of it.</hi> Though they cannot give an account of themselves (for there is <hi type="italic">no wisdom, nor device, nor knowledge at all in the grave,</hi> much less this), yet there is a world on the other side death and the grave, on which those dark regions border, and to which we must pass through them, and there we shall see clearly what we are now in the dark about. "Have a little patience," says Death to the inquisitive soul: "I will fetch thee shortly to a place where even this wisdom will be found." When <hi type="italic">the mystery of God shall be finished</hi> it will be laid open, and we shall know as we are known; when the veil of flesh is rent, and the interposing clouds are scattered, we shall know what God does, though we know not now, <reference osisRef="John.13.7">John xiii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen9938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9939" type="x-p"/> 2. This knowledge is hidden in God, as the apostle speaks, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Eph. iii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Known unto God are all his works,</hi> though they are not known to us, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.18">Acts xv. 18</reference>. There are good reasons for what he does, though we cannot assign them (<reference osisRef="Job.28.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">God understands the way thereof.</hi> Men sometimes do they know not what, but God never does. Men do what they did not design to do; new occurrences put them upon new counsels, and oblige them to take new measures. But God does all according to the purpose which he purposed in himself, and which he never alters. Men sometimes do that which they cannot give a good reason for, but in every will of God there is a counsel: he knows both what he does and why he does it, the whole series of events and the order and place of every occurrence. This knowledge he has in perfection, but keeps to himself. Two reasons are here given why God must needs understand his own way, and he only:— <div eID="gen9939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9940" type="x-p"/> (1.) Because all events are now directed by an all-seeing and almighty Providence, <reference osisRef="Job.28.24-Job.28.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. He that governs the world is, [1.] Omniscient; <hi type="italic">for he looks to the ends of the earth,</hi> both in place and time; distant ages, distant regions, are under his view. We do not understand our own way, much less can we understand God's way, because we are short-sighted. How little do we know of what is doing in the world, much less of what will be done? But <hi type="italic">the eyes of the Lord are in every place;</hi> nay, they <hi type="italic">run to and fro through the earth.</hi> Nothing is, or can be, hidden from him; and therefore the reasons why some wicked people prosper remarkably and others are remarkably punished in this world, which are secret to us, are known to him. One day's events, and one man's affairs, have such a reference to, and such a dependence upon, another's, that he only to whom all events and all affairs are naked and open, and who sees the whole at one entire and certain view, is a competent Judge of every part. [2.] He is omnipotent. He can do every thing, and is very exact in all he does. For proof of this Job mentions the winds and waters, <reference osisRef="Job.28.25">v. 25</reference>. What is lighter than the wind? Yet God hath ways of poising it. He knows how <hi type="italic">to make the weight for the winds,</hi> which he <hi type="italic">brings out of his treasuries</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>), keeping a very particular account of what he draws out, as men do of what they pay out of their treasuries, not at random, as men bring out their trash. Nothing sensible is to us more unaccountable than the wind. We <hi type="italic">hear the sound of it, yet cannot tell whence it comes, nor whither it goes;</hi> but God gives it out by weight, wisely ordering both from what point it shall blow and with what strength. The waters of the sea, and the rain-waters, he both weighs and measures, allotting the proportion of every tide and every shower. A great and constant communication there is between clouds and seas, the waters above the firmament and those under it. Vapours go up, rains come down, air is condensed into water, water rarefied into air; but the great God keeps an exact account of all the stock with which this trade is carried on for the public benefit and sees that none of it be lost. Now if, in these things, Providence be so exact, much more in dispensing frowns and favours, rewards and punishments, to the children of men, according to the rules of equity. <div eID="gen9940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9941" type="x-p"/> (2.) Because all events were from eternity designed and determined by an infallible prescience and immutable decree, <reference osisRef="Job.28.26-Job.28.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. When he settled the course of nature he foreordained all the operations of his government. [1.] He settled the course of nature. Job mentions particularly <hi type="italic">a decree for the rain</hi> and <hi type="italic">a way for the thunder and lightning.</hi> The general manner and method, and the particular uses and tendencies, of these strange performances, both their causes and their effects, were appointed by the divine purpose; hence God is said to <hi type="italic">prepare lightnings for the rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jer. x. 13</reference>. [2.] When he did that he laid all the measures of his providence, and drew an exact scheme of the whole work from first to last. Then, from eternity, did he see in himself, and declare to himself, the plan of his proceedings. Then he prepared it, fixed it, and established it, set every thing in readiness for all his works, so that, when any thing was to be done, nothing was to seek, nor could any thing unforeseen occur, to put it either out of its method or out of its time; for all was ordered as exactly as if he had studied it and searched it out, so that, whatever he does, <hi type="italic">nothing can be put to it nor taken from it,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">it shall be for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. Some make Job to speak of wisdom here as a person, and translate it, <hi type="italic">Then he saw her and showed her,</hi> &c., and then it is parallel with that of Solomon concerning the essential wisdom of the Father, the eternal Word, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.22-Prov.8.31">Prov. viii. 22</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">Before the earth was, then was I by him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.1-John.1.2">John i. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen9941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9942" type="x-p"/> II. The knowledge of God's revealed will, the will of his precept, and this is within our reach; it is level to our capacity, and will do us good (<reference osisRef="Job.28.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">Unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord that is wisdom.</hi> Let it not be said that when God concealed his counsels from man, and forbade him that tree of knowledge, it was because he grudged him any thing that would contribute to his real bliss and satisfaction; no, he let him know as much as he was concerned to know in order to his duty and happiness; he shall be entrusted with as much of his sovereign mind as is needful and fit for a subject, but he must not think himself fit to be a privy-counsellor. He said to <hi type="italic">Adam</hi> (so some), to the first man, in the day in which he was created; he told him plainly it was not for him to amuse himself with over-curious searches into the mysteries of creation, nor to pretend to solve all the phenomena of nature; he would find it neither possible nor profitable to do so. No less wisdom (says archbishop Tillotson) than that which made the world can thoroughly understand the philosophy of it. But let him look upon this as his wisdom, to fear the Lord and to depart from evil; let him learn that, and he is learned enough; let this knowledge serve his turn. When God forbade man the tree of knowledge he allowed him the tree of life, and this is that tree, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Prov. iii. 18</reference>. We cannot attain true wisdom but by divine revelation. <hi type="italic">The Lord giveth wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Prov. ii. 6</reference>. Now the matter of that is not found in the secrets of nature or providence, but in the rules for our own practice. Unto man he said, not, "Go up to heaven, to fetch happiness thence;" or, "Go down to the deep, to draw it up thence." No, <hi type="italic">the word is nigh thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.30.14">Deut. xxx. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">He hath shown thee, O man!</hi> not what is great, but <hi type="italic">what is good,</hi> not what the Lord thy God designs to do with thee, but what he <hi type="italic">requires of thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mic. vi. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Unto you, O men! I call,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.4">Prov. viii. 4</reference>. Lord, what is man that he should be thus minded, thus visited! Behold, mark, take notice of this; he that has ears let him hear what the God of heaven says to the children of men: <hi type="italic">The fear of the Lord, that is the wisdom.</hi> Here is, 1. The description of true religion, pure religion, and undefiled; it is to <hi type="italic">fear the Lord and depart from evil,</hi> which agrees with God's character of Job, <reference osisRef="Job.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>. The <hi type="italic">fear of the Lord</hi> is the spring and summary of all religion. There is a slavish fear of God, springing from hard thoughts of him, which is contrary to religion, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.24">Matt. xxv. 24</reference>. There is a selfish fear of God springing from dreadful thoughts of him, which may be a good step towards religion, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.5">Acts ix. 5</reference>. But there is a filial fear of God, springing from great and high thoughts of him, which is the life and soul of all religion. And, wherever this reigns in the heart, it will appear by a constant care to <hi type="italic">depart from evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.6">Prov. xvi. 6</reference>. This is essential to religion. We must first cease to do evil, or we shall never learn to do well. <hi type="italic">Virtus est vitium fugere—Even in our flight from vice some virtue lies.</hi> 2. The commendation of religion: it is <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> and <hi type="italic">understanding.</hi> To be truly religious is to be truly wise. As the wisdom of God appears in the institution of religion, so the wisdom of man appears in the practice and observance of it. It is understanding, for it is the best knowledge of truth; it is wisdom, for it is the best management of our affairs. Nothing more surely guides our way and gains our end than being religious.  <chapter eID="Job.28"/> <div eID="gen9942" type="x-p"/>

entries.4774716629e7c61d43b4c1a4d55252774e930f1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5041"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 28</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.28.1-Job.28.28">Job 28:1-28</reference>. Job's Speech Continued.</title> <div sID="gen7466" type="x-p"/> In the twenty-seventh chapter Job had tacitly admitted that the statement of the friends was often true, that God vindicated His justice by punishing the wicked here; but still the affliction of the godly remained unexplained. Man has, by skill, brought the precious metals from their concealment. But the Divine Wisdom, which governs human affairs, he cannot similarly discover (<reference osisRef="Job.28.12">Job 28:12</reference>, &c.). However, the image from the same metals (<reference osisRef="Job.23.10">Job 23:10</reference>) implies Job has made some way towards solving the riddle of his life; namely, that affliction is to him as the refining fire is to gold.<div eID="gen7466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5041"/><hi type="bold">1. vein--</hi>a mine, from which it goes forth, Hebrew, "is dug."<div eID="gen7467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">place for gold--</hi>a place where gold may be found, which men refine. Not as English Version, "A place--where," (Mal 3:3). Contrasted with gold found in the bed and sand of rivers, which does not need refining; as the gold dug from a mine does. Golden ornaments have been found in Egypt, of the times of Joseph. <div eID="gen7468" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb1c18efd9e042ef4fb74c575598adc84f8059f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5042"/><div sID="gen7469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5042"/><hi type="bold">2. brass--</hi>that is, copper; for brass is a mixed metal of copper and zinc, of modern invention. Iron is less easily discovered, and wrought, than copper; therefore copper was in common use long before iron. Copper-stone is called "cadmium" by Pliny [Natural History, 34:1; 36:21]. Iron is fitly said to be taken out of the "earth" (dust), for ore looks like mere earth. <div eID="gen7469" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5edd907f1714a109b941f23aa5bc57f12575f01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5043"/><div sID="gen7470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5043"/>3. "Man makes an end of darkness," by exploring the darkest depths (with torches).<div eID="gen7470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all perfection--</hi>rather, carries out his search to the utmost perfection; most thoroughly searches the stones of darkness and of the shadow of death (thickest gloom); that is, the stones, whatever they be, embedded in the darkest bowels of the earth [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Job.26.10">Job 26:10</reference>). <div eID="gen7471" type="x-p"/>
entries.96d84d6f1fac95853f8eb3ec1c858ded8d3671ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5044"/><div sID="gen7472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5044"/>4. Three hardships in mining: 1. "A stream (flood) breaks out at the side of the stranger"; namely, the miner, a strange newcomer into places heretofore unexplored; his surprise at the sudden stream breaking out beside him is expressed (English Version, "from the inhabitant"). 2. "Forgotten (unsupported) by the foot they hang," namely, by ropes, in descending. In the Hebrew, "Lo there" precedes this clause, graphically placing it as if before the eyes. "The waters" is inserted by English Version. "Are dried up," ought to be, "hang," "are suspended." English Version perhaps understood, waters of whose existence man was previously unconscious, and near which he never trod; and yet man's energy is such, that by pumps, &c., he soon causes them to "dry up and go away" [So Herder]. 3. "Far away from men, they move with uncertain step"; they stagger; not "they are gone" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7472" type="x-p"/>
entries.835e74bf2cedd558439d86a443e1f237fb708442: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5045"/><div sID="gen7473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5045"/>5. Its fertile surface yields food; and yet "beneath it is turned up as it were with fire." So Pliny [Natural History, 33] observes on the ingratitude of man who repays the debt he owes the earth for food, by digging out its bowels. "Fire" was used in mining [Umbreit]. English Version is simpler, which means precious stones which glow like fire; and so <reference osisRef="Job.28.6">Job 28:6</reference> follows naturally (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">Eze 28:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7473" type="x-p"/>
entries.f31e5b5fa75891feaeabe4284deae21cab333b5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5046"/><div sID="gen7474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5046"/>6. Sapphires are found in alluvial soil near rocks and embedded in gneiss. The ancients distinguished two kinds: 1. The real, of transparent blue: 2. That improperly so called, opaque, with gold spots; that is, lapis lazuli. To the latter, looking like gold dust, Umbreit refers "dust of gold." English Version better, "The stones of the earth are, &c., and the clods of it (Vulgate) are gold"; the parallel clauses are thus neater. <div eID="gen7474" type="x-p"/>
entries.98cc0203573f3bb4b96643bcb646bbdfc80b3723: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5047"/><div sID="gen7475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5047"/><hi type="bold">7. fowl--</hi>rather, "ravenous bird," or "eagle," which is the most sharp-sighted of birds (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">Is 46:11</reference>). A vulture will spy a carcass at an amazing distance. The miner penetrates the earth by a way unseen by birds of keenest sight. <div eID="gen7475" type="x-p"/>
entries.b539cdbe37091893a9193b83dbab70d35ba7cee1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5048"/><div sID="gen7476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5048"/><hi type="bold">8. lion's whelps--</hi>literally, "the sons of pride," that is, the fiercest beasts.<div eID="gen7476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passed--</hi>The Hebrew implies the proud gait of the lion. The miner ventures where not even the fierce lion dares to go in pursuit of his prey. <div eID="gen7477" type="x-p"/>
entries.287351768bc536e1c9b2450d985d18fa5afbd5ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5049"/><div sID="gen7478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5049"/><hi type="bold">9. rock--</hi>flint. He puts forth his hand to cleave the hardest rock.<div eID="gen7478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the roots--</hi>from their foundations, by undermining them. <div eID="gen7479" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0c1b0928e632f7a3da831e041d72d7c4b0236af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5050"/><div sID="gen7480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5050"/>10. He cuts channels to drain off the waters, which hinder his mining; and when the waters are gone, he he is able to see the precious things in the earth. <div eID="gen7480" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0b956b967f0eccf41bdc726d853f350cc851922: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5051"/><div sID="gen7481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5051"/><hi type="bold">11. floods--</hi>"He restrains the streams from weeping"; a poetical expression for the trickling subterranean rills, which impede him; answering to the first clause of <reference osisRef="Job.28.10">Job 28:10</reference>; so also the two latter clauses in each verse correspond. <div eID="gen7481" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb77173a0903bd72ca314ee11f300aa39a0d2bba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5052"/><div sID="gen7482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5052"/>12. Can man discover the Divine Wisdom by which the world is governed, as he can the treasures hidden in the earth? Certainly not. Divine Wisdom is conceived as a person (<reference osisRef="Job.28.12-Job.28.27">Job 28:12-27</reference>) distinct from God (<reference osisRef="Job.28.23">Job 28:23</reference>; also in <reference osisRef="Prov.8.23">Pr 8:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.27">27</reference>). The Almighty Word, Jesus Christ, we know now, is that Wisdom. The order of the world was originated and is maintained by the breathing forth (Spirit) of Wisdom, unfathomable and unpurchasable by man. In <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>, the only aspect of it, which relates to, and may be understood by, man, is stated.<div eID="gen7482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understanding--</hi>insight into the plan of the divine government. <div eID="gen7483" type="x-p"/>
entries.39b54565aa3f058c714b710328ae5eb425ba8ded: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5053"/><div sID="gen7484" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5053"/>13. Man can fix no price upon it, as it is nowhere to be found in man's abode (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.11">Is 38:11</reference>). Job implies both its valuable worth, and the impossibility of buying it at any price. <div eID="gen7484" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4776468cc697acc059af83f68239605c7629e54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5054"/><div sID="gen7485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5054"/>15. Not the usual word for "gold"; from a Hebrew root, "to shut up" with care; that is, purest gold (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.20">1Ki 6:20</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen7485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weighed--</hi>The precious metals were weighed out before coining was known (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.16">Ge 23:16</reference>). <div eID="gen7486" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fa432ea379eb189960b3b9cfbf9cb82fe5eec0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5055"/><div sID="gen7487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5055"/><hi type="bold">16. gold of Ophir--</hi>the most precious (See on <reference osisRef="Job.22.24">Job 22:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>).<div eID="gen7487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">onyx--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.2.12">Ge 2:12</reference>). More valued formerly than now. The term is Greek, meaning "thumb nail," from some resemblance in color. The Arabic denotes, of two colors, white preponderating. <div eID="gen7488" type="x-p"/>
entries.e85f092cba5ca7152ec02d737a0f6142a5fd0f41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5056"/><div sID="gen7489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5056"/><hi type="bold">17. crystal--</hi>Or else glass, if then known, very costly. From a root, "to be transparent."<div eID="gen7489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">jewels--</hi>rather, "vessels." <div eID="gen7490" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ac8ec8cf87ea9780ed567410c4d8823f2341213: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5057"/><div sID="gen7491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5057"/>18. Red coral (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">Eze 27:16</reference>).<div eID="gen7491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pearls--</hi>literally, "what is frozen." Probably crystal; and <reference osisRef="Job.28.17">Job 28:17</reference> will then be glass.<div eID="gen7492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rubies--</hi>Umbreit translates "pearls" (see <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">La 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.15">Pr 3:15</reference>). The Urim and Thummim, the means of consulting God by the twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate, "the stones of the sanctuary" (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">La 4:1</reference>), have their counterpart in this chapter; the precious stones symbolizing the "light" and "perfection" of the divine wisdom. <div eID="gen7493" type="x-p"/>
entries.c654923d269dda94360118133c7d4d601da6618b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5058"/><div sID="gen7494" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5058"/><hi type="bold">19. Ethiopia--</hi>Cush in the Hebrew. Either Ethiopia, or the south of Arabia, near the Tigris. <div eID="gen7494" type="x-p"/>
entries.377c6605b206a34e1de20bca4b30c162ec061a8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5059"/><div sID="gen7495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5059"/>20. <reference osisRef="Job.28.12">Job 28:12</reference> repeated with great force. <div eID="gen7495" type="x-p"/>
entries.186b284ddff516497b1e8963215e1666b78e1fb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5060"/><div sID="gen7496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5060"/>21. None can tell whence or where, seeing it, &c.<div eID="gen7496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fowls--</hi>The gift of divination was assigned by the heathen especially to birds. Their rapid flight heavenwards and keen sight originated the superstition. Job may allude to it. Not even the boasted divination of birds has an insight into it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.20">Ec 10:20</reference>). But it may merely mean, as in <reference osisRef="Job.28.7">Job 28:7</reference>, It escapes the eye of the most keen-sighted bird. <div eID="gen7497" type="x-p"/>
entries.abf2f0c5dbf927db77c99774954e4f8fa14722cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5061"/><div sID="gen7498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5061"/>22. That is, the abodes of destruction and of the dead. "Death" put for Sheol (<reference osisRef="Job.30.23">Job 30:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">26:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.13">Psa 9:13</reference>).<div eID="gen7498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We have [only] heard--</hi>the report of her. We have not seen her. In the land of the living (<reference osisRef="Job.28.13">Job 28:13</reference>) the workings of Wisdom are seen, though not herself. In the regions of the dead she is only heard of, her actings on nature not being seen (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>). <div eID="gen7499" type="x-p"/>
entries.12aa14130a0263ccc1be2f19178b6bc1f0fe2dd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5062"/><div sID="gen7500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5062"/>23. God hath, and is Himself, wisdom. <div eID="gen7500" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae919bbcd800240a71bd1ede17b0ad6ebd8b4202: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5063"/><div sID="gen7501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5063"/>24. "Seeth (all that is) under," &c. <div eID="gen7501" type="x-p"/>
entries.90ddf2c35ad75c056c4958441349f63a9a865dc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5064"/><div sID="gen7502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5064"/>25. God has adjusted the weight of the winds, so seemingly imponderable, lest, if too weighty, or too light, injury should be caused. He measureth out the waters, fixing their bounds, with wisdom as His counsellor (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.27-Prov.8.31">Pr 8:27-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Is 40:12</reference>). <div eID="gen7502" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d2deeec072ad1acdea7e744c652bfe09a1f6348: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5065"/><div sID="gen7503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5065"/>26. The decree regulating at what time and place, and in what quantity, the rain should fall.<div eID="gen7503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a way--</hi>through the parted clouds (<reference osisRef="Job.38.25">Job 38:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zec 10:1</reference>). <div eID="gen7504" type="x-p"/>
entries.f437faac9eea9ff11bf788983c901511980dd82c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5066"/><div sID="gen7505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5066"/><hi type="bold">27. declare--</hi>manifest her, namely, in His works (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.1">Psa 19:1</reference>, 2). So the approval bestowed by the Creator on His works (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.10">Ge 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.31">31</reference>); compare the "rejoicing" of wisdom at the same (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Pr 8:30</reference>; which Umbreit translates; "I was the skilful artificer by His side").<div eID="gen7505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepared--</hi>not created, for wisdom is from everlasting (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.22-Prov.8.31">Pr 8:22-31</reference>); but "established" her as Governor of the world.<div eID="gen7506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">searched ... out--</hi>examined her works to see whether she was adequate to the task of governing the world [Maurer]. <div eID="gen7507" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5b719cecf346139dde2fef267ea56ce1a7f78e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5067"/><div sID="gen7508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5067"/>28. Rather, "But unto man," &c. My wisdom is that whereby all things are governed; Thy wisdom is in fearing God and shunning evil, and in feeling assured that My wisdom always acts aright, though thou dost not understand the principle which regulates it; for example, in afflicting the godly (<reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>). The friends, therefore, as not comprehending the Divine Wisdom, should not infer Job's guilt from his sufferings. Here alone in Job the name of God, Adonai, occurs; "Lord" or "master," often applied to Messiah in Old Testament. Appropriately here, in speaking of the Word or Wisdom, by whom the world was made (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.22-Prov.8.31">Pr 8:22-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.3">Joh 1:3</reference>; Ecclesiasticus 24:1-34). <chapter eID="Job.28"/>

entries.2f0dc0615b70d44fb8342996c1058d1899acd623: <div eID="gen17211" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17212" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17213" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17213" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17212" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17214" type="x-p"/> Job, in showing the vanity of human pursuits in reference to genuine wisdom, mentions mining for and refining gold and silver, <reference osisRef="Job.28.1">Job 28:1</reference>; iron and other minerals, <reference osisRef="Job.28.2">Job 28:2</reference>; the difficulties of mining, <reference osisRef="Job.28.3">Job 28:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.4">Job 28:4</reference>; produce of grain for bread from the earth, and stones of fire from under it, <reference osisRef="Job.28.5">Job 28:5</reference>. He speaks of precious stones and gold dust, <reference osisRef="Job.28.6">Job 28:6</reference>; of the instinct of fowls and wild beasts in finding their way, <reference osisRef="Job.28.7">Job 28:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.8">Job 28:8</reference>; and of the industry and successful attempts of men in mining and other operations, <reference osisRef="Job.28.9-Job.28.11">Job 28:9-11</reference> : but shows that with all their industry, skill, and perseverance, they cannot find out true wisdom, <reference osisRef="Job.28.12">Job 28:12</reference>; of which he gives the most exalted character, <reference osisRef="Job.28.13-Job.28.22">Job 28:13-22</reference>; and shows that God alone, the fountain of wisdom, knows and can teach it, <reference osisRef="Job.28.24-Job.28.27">Job 28:24-27</reference>; and in what this true wisdom consists, <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>. <div eID="gen17214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17215" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17216" type="x-p"/> Surely there is a vein for the silver - This chapter is the oldest and finest piece of natural history in the world, and gives us very important information on several curious subjects; and could we ascertain the precise meaning of all the original words, we might, most probably, find out allusions to several useful arts which we are apt to think are of modern, or comparatively modern, invention. The word מוצא motsa, which we here translate vein, signifies literally, a going out; i.e., a mine, or place dug in the earth, whence the silver ore is extracted. And this ore lies generally in veins or loads, running in certain directions. <div eID="gen17216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17217" type="x-p"/> A place for gold where they fine it - This should rather be translated, A place for gold which they refine. Gold ore has also its peculiar mine, and requires to be refined from earthy impurities.
entries.5a907705ff4abeabf57e8c02b8c14881738532b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17218" type="x-p"/> Iron is taken out of the earth - This most useful metal is hidden under the earth, and men have found out the method of separating it from its ore. <div eID="gen17218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17219" type="x-p"/> Brass is molten out of the stone - As brass is a factitious metal, copper must be the meaning of the Hebrew word נחושה nechusah: literally, the stone is poured out for brass. If we retain the common translation, perhaps the process of making brass may be that to which Job refers; for this metal is formed from copper melted with the stone calamine; and thus the stone is poured out to make brass.
entries.37a26884fa37f9a35a05d9585e9d6d8f3bdf2a4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17220" type="x-p"/> He setteth an end to darkness - As it is likely Job still refers to mining, the words above may be understood as pointing out the persevering industry of man in penetrating into the bowels of the earth, in order to seek for metals and precious stones. Even the stones that lay hidden in the bowels of the earth he has digged for and brought to light, and has penetrated in directions in which the solar light could not be transmitted; so that he appears to have gone to the regions of the shadow of death. Mr. Good translates: "Man delveth into the region of darkness; and examineth, to the uttermost limit, the stones of darkness and death-shade."
entries.c0370eb8c804084ee50e1d222bad57648b74643a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17221" type="x-p"/> The flood breaketh out from the inhabitant - This passage is very difficult. Some think it refers to mining; others to navigation. If it refer to the former, it may be intended to point out the waters that spring up when the miners have sunk down to a considerable depth, so that the mine is drowned, and they are obliged to give it up. Previously to the invention of the steam-engine this was generally the case: hence ancient mines may be reopened and worked to great advantage, because we have the means now to take off the water which the ancient workers had not. When, therefore, floods break out in those shafts, they are abandoned; and thus they are, <div eID="gen17221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17222" type="x-p"/> Forgotten of the foot - No man treads there any more. The waters increase דלו dallu, they are elevated, they rise up to a level with the spring, or till they meet with some fissure by which they can escape; and thence מאנוש נעו meenosh nau, they are moved or carried away from men; the stream is lost in the bowels of the earth. <div eID="gen17222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17223" type="x-p"/> Mr. Peters thinks that both this verse, and <reference osisRef="Job.9.26">Job 9:26</reference>, refer to navigation, then in a state of infancy; for the sea is not so much as mentioned; but נחל nachal, a torrent or flood, some river or arm of the sea perhaps of a few leagues over, which, dividing the several nations, must interrupt their hospitality and commerce with each other, unless by the help of navigation. According to this opinion the verse may be translated and paraphrased thus: The flood-rivers and arms of the sea - separateth from the stranger, מעם ג meim gar, divides different nations and peoples: they are forgotten of the foot - they cannot walk over these waters, they must embark in vessels; then they dwindle away, דלו dallu, from the size of men, that is, in proportion to their departure from the land they lessen on the sight; נעו nau, they are tossed up and down, namely, by the action of the waves. This receives some countenance from the psalmist's fine description, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.26">Psa 107:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.27">Psa 107:27</reference>, of a ship in a rough sea: They mount up to heaven; they go down again to the depths: their soul is melted because of trouble. They reel to and fro, ינועו yanuu, (the same word as above), they stagger like a drunken man. Mr. Good's translation is singular: - <div eID="gen17223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17224" type="x-p"/> He breaketh up the veins from the matrice, <div eID="gen17224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17225" type="x-p"/> Which, though thought nothing of under the foot, <div eID="gen17225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17226" type="x-p"/> Are drawn forth, are brandished among mankind. <div eID="gen17226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17227" type="x-p"/> This learned man thinks that it applies solely to mining, of which I cannot doubt; and therefore I adopt the first interpretation: but as to agreement among translators, it will be sought in vain. I shall just add Coverdale: With the ryver of water parteth he a sunder the straunge people, that knoweth no good neighbourheade; such as are rude, unmannerly, and boysterous.
entries.d0682dd153254eff0f9790f2e7a7e263646da476: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17228" type="x-p"/> The earth, out of it cometh bread - Or the earth, ממנה mimmennah, from itself, by its own vegetative power, it sends out bread, or the corn of which bread is made. <div eID="gen17228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17229" type="x-p"/> And under it is turned up as it were fire - It seems as if this referred to some combustible fossil, similar to our stone coal, which was dug up out of the earth in some places of Arabia. The Chaldee gives a translation, conformable to a very ancient opinion, which supposed the center of the earth to be a vast fire, and the place called hell. "The earth from which food proceeds, and under which is gehenna, whose cold snow is converted into the likeness of fire; and the garden of Eden, which is the place whose stones are sapphires," etc. The Vulgate has, "The land from which bread has been produced has been destroyed by fire." If this be the meaning of the original, there is probably an allusion to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; and the seventh and eighth verses may be supposed to refer to that catastrophe, there being no place left tangible or visible where those cities once stood: neither fowl nor beast could discern a path there, the whole land being covered with the lake Asphaltites.
entries.4c87236dc25115dc29c657e6bbf1e743550a4cbc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17230" type="x-p"/> The stones - the place of sapphires - In the language of mineralogists, the gangue, matrix, or bed in which the sapphire is found. For a description of this stone, see on <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference> (note). <div eID="gen17230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17231" type="x-p"/> Dust of gold - Or rather, gold dust.
entries.ad5c4ca8ec83e4dd27e23de662c76414fbe911fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17232" type="x-p"/> There is a path which no fowl knoweth - The instinct of birds is most surprising. They traverse vast forests, etc., in search of food, at a great distance from the place which they have chosen for their general residence; and return in all weathers, never missing their track: they also find their own nest without ever mistaking another of the same kind for it. Birds of passage, also, after tarrying in a foreign clime for six or seven months, return to their original abode over kingdoms and oceans, without missing their way, or deviating in the least from the proper direction; not having a single object of sight to direct their peregrinations. In such cases even the keen scent of the vulture, and the quick, piercing sight of the eagle, would be of no use. It is possible that Job may here refer to undiscovered mines and minerals; that notwithstanding man had already discovered much, yet much remained undiscovered, especially in the internal structure and contents of the earth. Since his time innumerable discoveries have been made; and yet how little do we know! Our various conflicting and contradictory theories of the earth are full proofs of our ignorance, and strong evidences of our folly. The present dogmatical systems of geology itself are almost the ne plus ultra of brain-sick visionaries, and system-mad mortals. They talk as confidently of the structure of the globe, and the manner and time in which all was formed, as if they had examined every part from the center to the circumference; though not a soul of man has ever penetrated two miles in perpendicular depth into the bowels of the earth. And with this scanty, defective knowledge, they pretend to build systems of the universe, and blaspheme the revelation of God! Poor souls! All these things are to them a path which no fowl knoweth, which the vulture's eye hath not seen, on which the lion's whelps have not trodden, and by which the fierce lion have not passed. The wisdom necessary to such investigations is out of their reach; and they have not simplicity of heart to seek it where it may be found. One of the Chaldee Targums gives a strange turn to this verse: - "The path of the tree of life Sammael, (Satan), though flying like a bird, hath not known; nor hath the eye of Eve beheld it. The children of men have not walked in it; nor hath the serpent turned towards it."
entries.54535b4be925019126dcfcc8b84d37c18c968bc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17233" type="x-p"/> He putteth forth his hand upon the rock, - Still there appears to be a reference to mining. Man puts his hand upon the rock, he breaks that to pieces, in order to extract the metals which it contains. <div eID="gen17233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17234" type="x-p"/> He overturneth the mountains - He excavates, undermines, or digs them away, when in search of the metals contained in them: this is not only poetically, but literally, the case in many instances.
entries.a96cfc0a3a8a5c60bb899b6dd0663bf30e9db2d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17235" type="x-p"/> He cutteth out rivers among the rocks - He cuts canals, adits, etc., in the rocks, and drives levels under ground, in order to discover loads or veins of ore. These are often continued a great way under ground; and may be poetically compared to rivers, channels, or canals. <div eID="gen17235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17236" type="x-p"/> His eye seeth every precious thing - He sinks those shafts, and drives those levels, in order to discover where the precious minerals lie, of which he is in pursuit.
entries.5048b3658dc04591b08fdf0614432c4ef7e423d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17237" type="x-p"/> He bindeth the floods - Prevents the risings of springs from drowning the mines; and conducts rivers and streams from their wonted course, in order to bring forth to light what was hidden under their beds. The binding or restraining the water, which, at different depths, annoys the miner, is both difficult and expensive: in some cases it may be drawn off by pipes or canals into neighboring water courses; in others, it is conducted to one receptacle or reservoir, and thence drawn off. In Europe it is generally done by means of steam-engines. What method the ancients had in mining countries, we cannot tell; but they dug deep in order to find out the riches of the earth. Pliny says, nervously, Imus in viscera terrae; et in sede manium opes quaerimus. "We descend into the bowels of the earth; and seek for wealth even in the abodes of departed spirits." The manes or ghosts of the dead, or spirits presiding over the dead, were supposed to have their habitation in the center of the earth; or in the deepest pits and caves. Ovid, speaking of the degeneracy of men in the iron age, Met. lib. i., ver. 137, says: - <div eID="gen17237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17238" type="x-p"/> Nec tantum segetes alimentaque debita dives <div eID="gen17238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17239" type="x-p"/> Poscebatur humus; sed itum est in viscera terrae: <div eID="gen17239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17240" type="x-p"/> Quasque recondiderat, Stygiisque admoverat umbris, <div eID="gen17240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17241" type="x-p"/> Effodiuntur opes, irritaenenta malorum. <div eID="gen17241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17242" type="x-p"/> Jamque nocens ferrum, ferroque nocentius aurum <div eID="gen17242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17243" type="x-p"/> Prodierat: prodit bellum, quod pugnat utroque; <div eID="gen17243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17244" type="x-p"/> Sanguineaque manu crepitantia concutit arma. "Nor was the ground alone required to bear <div eID="gen17244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17245" type="x-p"/> Her annual income to the crooked share: <div eID="gen17245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17246" type="x-p"/> But greedy mortals, rummaging her store, <div eID="gen17246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17247" type="x-p"/> Digg'd from her entrails first the precious ore; <div eID="gen17247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17248" type="x-p"/> And that alluring ill to sight display'd, <div eID="gen17248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17249" type="x-p"/> Which, next to hell, the prudent gods had laid. <div eID="gen17249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17250" type="x-p"/> Thus cursed steel, and more accursed gold, <div eID="gen17250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17251" type="x-p"/> Gave mischief birth, and made that mischief bold; <div eID="gen17251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17252" type="x-p"/> And double death did wretched man invade, <div eID="gen17252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17253" type="x-p"/> By steel assaulted, and by gold betray'd." <div eID="gen17253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17254" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen17254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17255" type="x-p"/> By binding the floods from overflowing, some have supposed that there is an allusion to the flux and reflux of the sea. In its flowing it is so bound, has its bounds assigned by the Most High, that it does not drown the adjacent country; and in its ebbing the parts which are ordinarily covered with the water are brought to view.
entries.17c31bb26a74d70e6a36419d120f96232a95b3e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17256" type="x-p"/> But where shall wisdom be found? - It is most evident that the terms wisdom and understanding are used here in a widely different sense from all those arts and sciences which have their relation to man in his animal and social state, and from all that reason and intellect by which man is distinguished from all other animals. Now as these terms חכמה chochmah, wisdom, and בינה binah, understanding or discernment, are often applied in the sacred writings in their common acceptations, we must have recourse to what Job says of them, to know their meaning in this place. In <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>, he says, The fear of the Lord is Wisdom, and to depart from evil is Understanding. We know that the fear of the Lord is often taken for the whole of that religious reverence and holy obedience which God prescribes to man in his word, and which man owes to his Maker. Hence the Septuagint render חכמה chochmah, wisdom, by θεοσεβια, Divine worship; and as to a departure from evil, that is necessarily implied in a religious life, but it is here properly distinguished, that no man might suppose that a right faith, and a proper performance of the rites of religious worship, is the whole of religion. No. They must not only worship God in the letter, but also in the spirit; they must not only have the form, but also the power of godliness: and this will lead them to worship God in spirit and truth, to walk in his testimonies, and abstain from every appearance of evil; hence they will be truly happy: so that wisdom is another word for happiness. Now these are things which man by study and searching could never find out; they are not of an earthly origin. The spirit of a man, human understanding, may know the things of a man - those which concern him in his animal and social state: but the Spirit of God alone knows the things of God; and therefore Wisdom - all true religion - must come by Divine revelation, which is the mode of its attainment. Wisdom finds out the thing, and understanding uses and applies the means; and then the great end is obtained.
entries.77a2eb37a04fdca19e3d571ad4bcceb4e5a481f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17257" type="x-p"/> Man knoweth not the price thereof - It is of infinite value; and is the only science which concerns both worlds. Without it, the wisest man is but a beast; with it, the simplest man is next to an angel. <div eID="gen17257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17258" type="x-p"/> Neither is it found in the land of the living - The world by wisdom, its wisdom, never knew God. True religion came by Divine revelation: that alone gives the true notion of God, his attributes, ways, designs, judgments, providences, etc., whence man came, what is his duty, his nature, and his end. Literature, science, arts, etc., etc., can only avail man for the present life, nor can they contribute to his true happiness, unless tempered and directed by genuine religion.
entries.05e130769c0d7e454fcf647735ed233ed7266117: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17259" type="x-p"/> The depth saith, It is not in me - Men may dig into the bowels of the earth, and there find gold, silver, and precious stones; but these will not give them true happiness. <div eID="gen17259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17260" type="x-p"/> The sea saith, It is not with me - Men may explore foreign countries, and by navigation connect as it were the most distant parts of the earth, and multiply the comforts and luxuries of life; but every voyage and every enjoyment proclaim, True happiness is not here.
entries.07b87b8d71e32bb45dcc16c57d94015e24044f4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17261" type="x-p"/> It cannot be gotten for gold - Genuine religion and true happiness are not to be acquired by earthly property. Solomon made gold and silver as plentiful as the stones in Jerusalem, and had all the delights of the sons of men, and yet he was not happy; yea, he had wisdom, was the wisest of men, but he had not the wisdom of which Job speaks here, and therefore, to him, all was vanity and vexation of spirit. If Solomon, as some suppose, was the author of this book, the sentiments expressed here are such as we might expect from this deeply experienced and wise man.
entries.3751d5815714a2a534ba1cc2f654a893f6c5dcd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17262" type="x-p"/> The gold of Ophir - Gold is five times mentioned in this and <reference osisRef="Job.28.17">Job 28:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.28.19">Job 28:19</reference>, and four of the times in different words. I shall consider them all at once. <div eID="gen17262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17263" type="x-p"/> 1. סגור Segor, from סגר sagar, to shut up. Gold. in the mine, or shut up in the ore; native gold washed by the streams out of the mountains, etc.; unwrought gold. <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference> <div eID="gen17263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17264" type="x-p"/> 2. כתם Kethem, from כתם catham, to sign or stamp: gold made current by being coined, or stamped with its weight or value; what we would call standard or sterling gold. <reference osisRef="Job.28.17">Job 28:17</reference> <div eID="gen17264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17265" type="x-p"/> 3. זהב Zahab, from זהב zahab, to be Lear, bright, or resplendent: the untarnishing metal; the only metal that always keeps its lustre. But probably here it means gold chased, or that in which precious stones are set; burnished gold. <div eID="gen17265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17266" type="x-p"/> 4. פז Paz, from פז paz, to consolidate, joined here with כלי keley, vessels, ornaments, instruments, etc.: hammered or wrought gold; gold in the finest forms, and most elegant utensils. This metal is at once the brightest, most solid, and most precious, of all the metals yet discovered, of which we have no less than forty in our catalogues. In these verses there are also seven kinds of precious stones, etc., mentioned: onyx, sapphire, crystal, coral, pearls, rubies, and topaz. <div eID="gen17266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17267" type="x-p"/> These I shall also consider in the order of their occurrence. <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference> <div eID="gen17267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17268" type="x-p"/> 1. שהם shoham, the Onyx, from ονυξ, a man's nail, hoof of a horse, because in color it resembles both. This stone is a species of chalcedony; and consists of alternate layers of white and brown chalcedony, under which it generally ranges. In the Vulgate it is called sardonyx, compounded of sard and onyx. Sard is also a variety of chalcedony, of a deep reddish-brown color, of which, and alternate layers of milk-white chalcedony, the sardonyx consists. A most beautiful block of this mineral sardonyx, from Iceland, now lies before me. <div eID="gen17268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17269" type="x-p"/> 2. ספיר sappir, the Sapphire stone, From ספר saphar, to count, number; probably from the number of golden spots with which it is said the sapphire of the ancients abounded. Pliny says, Hist. Nat. lib. xxxvii., cap. 8: Sapphirus aureis punctis collucet: coeruleae et sapphiri, raraque cum purpura: optimae apud Medos, nusquam tame perlucidae. "The sapphire glitters with golden spots. Sapphires are sometimes of an azure, never of a purple color. Those of Media are the best, but there are none transparent."
