                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and he knoweth the place thereof <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Where it dwells, which is only in his own Breast and Mind, and in the best of men but in part, and only as far as it pleaseth him to afford it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24. For he looketh to the ends of the Earth, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> seeth under the whole heaven <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He, and he only knows it, because his Providence, and that only, is infinite and universal, reaching to all places, and times, and things, past, present, and to come; whereas the most acute and knowing men have narrow understandings, and see but very few things, and small parcels of the works of God, and therefore are very unfit to pass a judgment upon them, because the Wisdom, and Justice, and Beauty of Gods works is not clearly nor fully seen till all the parts of them be laid together.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:409" />25. To make the weight for the winds <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which of themselves are most light, and without any weight, and inconstant, and such as no Creature can order or govern them: But God manageth them all by weight, appointing to every Wind that blows, its season, its proportion, its bounds and limits, when, and where, and how much, and how long each Wind shall blow, and for what ends, whether for Mercy, as to refresh men in hot seasons with its gentle gales, to cherish the fruits of the Earth, to waft Ships on the Sea to their desired Havens, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> or whether for Judgment, as to corrupt the air, and thereby the Bodies of men, and Fruits of the Earth, to blow down Houses upon their Inhabi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tants, as he was pleased to deal with my poor unhappy Children. He only doth all these things, and he only knows why he doth them. He instanceth but in some few of Gods works, and those which seem to be most trivial, and casual, and uncertain, that thereby he might more strongly imply and prove that God doth the same in other things which are more considerable, and are mana<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged by more constant causes, and certain methods, that he doth all things in the most exact order, and weight, and measure.</ns0:note>, and he weigheth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">But it seems a very improper speech, <ns0:hi>to weigh</ns0:hi> things <ns0:hi>by measure,</ns0:hi> and therefore this word may more fitly be otherwise rendred, <ns0:hi>he examineth,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>disposeth,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>fitteth,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>directeth,</ns0:hi> for so this verb is elsewhere used, as 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 3. <ns0:hi>Psal</ns0:hi> 75. 3. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 16. 2. & 21. 2.</ns0:note> the waters <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To wit, the Rain-waters, as appears from the next Verse, which God layeth up in his Store-houses, or bottles, the Clouds, and thence draws them forth, and sends them down upon the Earth in such times and proportions as he thinks fit, and as may serve his se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral designs and ends.</ns0:note> by measure <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">For liquid things are examined by mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure, as other things are by weight: and here is both <ns0:hi>weight</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>measure</ns0:hi> to signifie with what exact and perfect Wisdom God doth govern the World.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26. When he made <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Which was either from eternity, or at the first Creation, when he settled that course and order which should afterwards be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinued. Or, <ns0:hi>when he maketh:</ns0:hi> But our Translation seems best to suit with the <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> in the next Verse, where the sense is compleated.</ns0:note> a decree for the rain <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">An appointment, and as it were a Statute Law, that it should fall upon the Earth, and that in such times, and places, and propor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, and manner, as he should think fit, either <ns0:hi>for correction,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>for mercy,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Elihu</ns0:hi> speaks, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 37. 13.</ns0:note>, and a way <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>path,</ns0:hi> how it should get out of the thick Cloud in which it was shut up, and as it were im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prisoned: or, <ns0:hi>a course,</ns0:hi> which should for the future be observed, as to the time, and measure, and ends, and other circumstances be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longing to it.</ns0:note> for the lightning of the thunder.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27. Then <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either from eternity, when he decreed what he would do, or when he first created them.</ns0:note> did he see it <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Wisdom, which is the subject matter of the present discourse. This God <ns0:hi>saw</ns0:hi> not abroad, but within himself, he looked or reflected upon it in his own mind, as the rule by which he would proceed in the Creation and Government of all things, managing them in such ways and me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thods as were most agreeable to his own most wise and unsearch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able Counsels, which no humane or created Wit can reach or pierce into. Or, he <ns0:hi>saw</ns0:hi> it so as to declare it, as it follows, so as to make it visible and manifest in some measure to his Creatures. Or, he <ns0:hi>saw it, i. e.</ns0:hi> he enjoyed it, <ns0:hi>seeing</ns0:hi> being oft put for <ns0:hi>enjoying,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 27. 13. & 34. 12. <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 3. 13. & 2. 1. Compare <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 8. 22.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> number it.</ns0:note> declare it <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He made it evident, he discovered his deep Wisdom which lay hid before in his own breast; or he laid the founda<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of that discovery of it, which then was, or afterward should be made to Angels and Men, as the <ns0:hi>Heavens</ns0:hi> did in themselves <ns0:hi>de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clare the glory of God,</ns0:hi> Psal. 19. 1. before there was such a Creature as man to take notice of it, because the object was visible in itself, and not made so by the Eye which afterwards beheld it. Or, <ns0:hi>did number it, i. e.</ns0:hi> shewed it as it were by number, not only in gross, but as it were by retail, in all the several works which he made.</ns0:note>, he prepared it <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He had it in readiness for the doing of all his works, as if he had been for a long time preparing materials for them. So it is a speech of God after the manner of men. Or, <ns0:hi>he disposed it, i. e.</ns0:hi> used or employed it in his works. Or, he <ns0:hi>settled,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>established it, i. e.</ns0:hi> he firmly purposed to do such and such things in such manner as he thought meet, and he established the order which he first made in the World, that it should continue in after ages. Or, <ns0:hi>he directed it,</ns0:hi> and directed and ordered all things by it.</ns0:note>, yea, and searched it out <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Not properly; for so searching implies Ignorance, and that a man is at a loss, and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quires time and industry, all which is repugnant to the Divine Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections; but figuratively, as such expressions are oft used con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning God<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>i<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> e.</ns0:hi> He did, and doth, all things with that absolute and perfect Wisdom, and he knoweth all his own Counsels and Action<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, and the reasons of them, so exactly, and perfectly, as if he had bestowed a long time in searching, and judging, to find them out. And this, and the other Acts mentioned in this Verse, are to be understood of God solely and exclusively, it being here, as it is oft elsewhere in this Book, sufficiently implied, that this kind of divine Wisdom, which consists in the accurate knowledge of all Gods Counsels and works, is far above, out of man's reach: Man doth not <ns0:hi>see</ns0:hi> this Wisdom, but only so far as God is pleased to reveal it to him, and therefore he cannot <ns0:hi>declare</ns0:hi> it to others; man did not <ns0:hi>prepare,</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>order,</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>contri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> it, and therefore no wonder if he cannot <ns0:hi>search it out.</ns0:hi> And so this is most fitly connect<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with the following Verse: For as here he tells us what Wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom is denied to man, so there he informeth us what is granted to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. And <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>But:</ns0:hi> For this is added by way of opposition, to shew that mans Wisdom doth not lie in a curious enquiry into, or an exact knowledge of the secret paths of Gods Counsel and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vidence, but in things of another, and of a lower nature.</ns0:note> unto man <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> at first, and in, and with him, to all his Race and Poster<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty.</ns0:note> he said <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> God spake it, partly and at first inwardly to the mind of Man, in which God wrote this with his own Finger, and en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />graved it as a first Principle for his direction, and partly after<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards by the Holy Patriarchs, and Prophets, and other Teachers of his Church, whom God sent into the World to teach men true Wisdom; which accordingly they did, not by acquainting the People with the secrets and intricacies of Gods Counsel and Provi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence, but by declaring the revealed Will of God, and instruct<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing them in their duty towards God and Men, making this their great if not only business, to make men wise unto Salvation. See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4. 6. & 29. 29.</ns0:note>, behold <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Which expression notes the great import<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance of this Doctrine, and withal man's dulness and backwardness to apprehend and consider it, and man's proneness to place his Wisdom in vain and curious speculations.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                     </ns0:note> the fear of the LORD <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> True Religion, and the right Worship of God, both inward and outward, all which cometh under this name.</ns0:note>, that is wisdom <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">In that only consists mans true Wisdom, because that, and that only, is his duty, and his safety, and happiness, both for this Life and for the next, and withal this is attainable, whereas the depths of Gods ways are unknown, and unsearchable to humane or created Capacities.</ns0:note>, and to depart from evil <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, which is called <ns0:hi>evil</ns0:hi> eminently, as being the chief if not the only Evil, and the cause of all other evils, and that which is constantly and immutably evil, whereas afflictions are frequently made good and highly beneficial. Religion consists of two Branches, doing good, and forsaking evil; the former is expressed in the former clause of this Verse, and the latter in these words.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> understanding <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Is the best kind of Knowledge or Wisdom to which man can attain in this Life. The same thing is here twice expressed in several Phrases. And the design of <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> in this close of his Discourse, is not only to shew the mistake, and reprove the Arrogance and boldness of his Friends, in prying into Gods secrets, and passing such a rash censure upon him, and upon Gods ways and carriage towards him; but also to v<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ndicate himself from the imputation of Hypocrifie and Profaneness, which they fastened upon him, by shewing that he had ever esteemed it to be his best Wisdom, and true Interest, to fear God, and to depart from evil.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
